notable_claims: Locking a student's account in an academic setting can be tantamount to expulsion.
System administrators should operate under the principle of 'innocent until proven guilty'.
Good system administration should be as invisible as possible.
classification.summary: The author shares a personal account of data loss caused by a system administrator's arbitrary deletion of files to save disk space. He argues that university system administrators should view themselves as service providers and exercise extreme caution when using administrative power, such as locking accounts. The post emphasizes that in academic settings, losing computer access can be equivalent to expulsion from the educational process.
classification.title: War story and some thoughts....

notable_claims: System administrators are often unfairly targeted with blanket condemnations by users who do not understand the complexities of system management.
organizations: University of Kentucky Engineering Computing Center
classification.summary: Wes Morgan defends system administrators against criticisms voiced in the discussion group. He argues that users often lack an understanding of the technical and administrative burdens involved in managing shared computing resources. The post highlights common user behaviors that strain systems, such as excessive background jobs and disk space demands.
classification.title: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

identity.subject: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

notable_claims: Tension between students and admins stems from differing perceptions of system robustness and the legitimacy of exploratory behavior.
Students often apply a 'single-user' mentality to multi-user systems, underestimating the consequences of their actions.
System administrators prioritize infrastructure stability over user motive because damage can occur without malicious intent.
classification.summary: William Hugh Murray analyzes the psychological and perceptual gap between students and system administrators regarding computer use. He argues that students view systems as robust toys to be explored, while administrators view them as fragile infrastructure requiring strict protection. This divergence in perspective leads to conflict over 'exploratory' behavior versus security enforcement.
classification.title: Tension between student users and system administrators

notable_claims: OSU library administration believes in unregulated access to library materials.
Physical adult magazines at OSU are restricted by ID requirements primarily to prevent theft rather than to censor content.
organizations: Center for Advanced Study in Telecommunications
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the accessibility of adult materials at Ohio State University to contrast physical library policies with digital access. Jane Fraser reports that OSU librarians support unregulated access to materials, noting that adult magazines are available to anyone who can provide an ID. The conversation aims to challenge restrictive CIS policies by comparing them to established library standards.

notable_claims: Users have a right to protest unfair rules but not a right to violate them.
Severe punishments are often the result of follow-up infractions rather than original offenses.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides advice to computer users facing disciplinary action from system administrators. He warns against committing further rule infractions during protests of unfair rules, as follow-up offenses often lead to more severe punishments than the original act.
classification.title: How to back a user into a corner

identity.subject: Re: How to back a user into a corner

notable_claims: System abuse often stems from a lack of communication between systems staff and users.
Explaining the reasons behind system restrictions can reduce user frustration and increase support for those restrictions.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur, a systems administrator at SUNY Stony Brook, discusses the importance of communication between technical staff and users. He argues that system abuse is typically caused by a lack of communication rather than malice. He advocates for direct access to systems staff as a central element of institutional policy to reduce user frustration.
classification.title: Users and Systems staff interaction

notable_claims: Accounts were suspended during Internet and DECnet worm outbreaks if usernames matched passwords.
Account suspensions are primarily triggered automatically by a lack of allocated funds.
User files are archived upon account deletion if requested by the user.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur, a system administrator at SUNY Stony Brook, outlines the specific criteria used for suspending or deleting user accounts. He describes policies regarding funding exhaustion, security risks during worm outbreaks, and administrative departures. The post concludes by questioning if these standard practices constitute 'wrongful' denials of service.

User participation in policy formulation increases the perceived legitimacy of those policies.
Peer representation on policy committees is generally more beneficial for students than no representation.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the necessity of due process and student participation in the creation of university computer policies. Academic transcripts should contain only information about academic status, keeping disciplinary records separate.

The participants debate whether computing privileges can be suspended pending a hearing and whether disciplinary records for computer infractions should appear on academic transcripts.

notable_claims: System administrators should not be the ones to punish students.
Permanent expulsion from a computer system is inappropriate if access is necessary for coursework.
There is no significant distinction between access to academic libraries and access to academic computers regarding student punishment.
classification.summary: Peter D. Junger argues that system administrators should not have the authority to punitively expel students from computer systems, as such actions bypass due process. He contends that access to academic computers is as essential for coursework as access to libraries and should therefore be managed by formal university disciplinary bodies. He suggests administrators act only as witnesses in complaints rather than judges.
classification.title: Re: Punishment
